text.paragraph: New painless lump under the left nipple in a man of 51. Concerns: Found a small, painless lump under the left nipple in the shower a few days ago; at first put it down to the breast enlargement he had at 13; Embarrassed to bring up a breast lump and did not think a man could have breast cancer; worried that a diagnosis could cost him work and wants it kept private. [S]

tr.td: Diagnostic mammography of both breasts: 1.6 cm irregular, spiculated retroareolar mass eccentric to the left nipple (BI-RADS 5); right breast with no mass and no gynecomastia (BI-RADS 1)

Ultrasound of both breasts and both axillae: 1.5 cm irregular hypoechoic mass with angular margins next to the left nipple; one left axillary lymph node with a thickened cortex; right breast and right axilla normal

Ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy of the left breast mass and the left axillary node: invasive ductal carcinoma, grade 3; estrogen receptor 95 percent, progesterone receptor 85 percent, HER2 1+ (negative), Ki-67 30 percent; the node contains metastatic carcinoma

Mastectomy with level I and II axillary lymph node dissection for left breast cancer. Pathology of the left breast: invasive ductal carcinoma 1.6 cm, grade 3, margins clear, no lymphovascular invasion; 2 of 15 lymph nodes involved (largest 7 mm), no extranodal extension; pT1c pN1a, stage IIA
Transthoracic echocardiogram before anthracycline chemotherapy: left ventricular ejection fraction 62 percent; normal valves and wall motion
Advance care planning conversation, about 20 minutes

Biopsy results: breast cancer; surgical oncology consultation; germline test and preparation for surgery
Review two weeks after mastectomy and axillary dissection: pathology, wound and arm care, and preparation for chemotherapy
Periodic adult preventive visit before chemotherapy

code.displayName: Periodic reevaluation and management of healthy individual

tr.td: Urgent surgical oncology (breast) consultation for a biopsy-proven, node-positive breast cancer, to plan the operation and the axilla
Same-week diagnostic mammography and ultrasound of both breasts and both axillae, and ultrasound-guided core biopsy of the mass and the abnormal node with ER, PR, and HER2 testing
Genetic counseling and germline multigene panel testing (including BRCA2, BRCA1, PALB2, CHEK2, and ATM), as for every man with breast cancer, with a letter for relatives if a variant is found
Mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection, then shoulder exercises and lymphedema risk reduction with arm measurements at each visit

Adjuvant chemotherapy given by medical oncology (doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide every three weeks for four cycles, then weekly paclitaxel for twelve weeks, about six months), after a baseline echocardiogram, hepatitis B screening, vaccines, and a dental review; radiation oncology review of post-mastectomy radiation after chemotherapy
Tamoxifen after chemotherapy for at least five years, the first-choice endocrine therapy for men, with venous thromboembolism, mood, hot flash, sexual side effect, and adherence checks at every visit
Distress screening at each visit, plain information that men get breast cancer, confidential handling of his diagnosis at work, and the offer of a peer-support group for men with breast cancer
Tissue diagnosis within one week of presentation
Imaging and core biopsy the day after presentation; diagnosis explained on the sixth day
Curative surgery within two weeks of diagnosis, with lymphedema prevention taught
Mastectomy and axillary dissection two days after the diagnosis; clear margins; arm exercises and risk reduction taught
Complete germline genetic testing with counseling before chemotherapy starts
Panel sent on the day of diagnosis; result not yet back at the end of the episode
Be ready to start adjuvant chemotherapy within six weeks of surgery: echocardiogram, hepatitis B screening, vaccines, and dental review done
Echocardiogram normal; vaccines and hepatitis B screening at the preventive visit; dental review booked; first cycle scheduled
